 The Explorer 100D is a palm-sized 30,000mAh portable power station 
 It uses a long-lasting lithium iron phosphate battery 
 It has a maximum total output of 158W and supports direct solar input 
 Jackery has just launched a new portable power station that combines a high capacity with an impressively small and lightweight design.
 Dubbed the Jackery Explorer 100D, it measures 11.87 x 8.26 x 8.57cm and weighs 850g, which sounds fairly compact when you consider that it has 30,000mAh of power. Indeed, it’s 14% smaller and 12% lighter than the Explorer 100 Plus, making it Jackery's smallest portable power station yet.
 So, while it will certainly add some weight to your bag, it's small enough to carry around in a backpack, so you can keep your devices powered when out and about or on trips. It’s designed to comply with lithium battery transport standards, too, so you can take it on planes and trains, and even though it’s palm-sized, it also includes a built-in handle and supports an optional shoulder strap.

 (Image credit: Jackery) An LFP battery with solar support
 The Jackery Explorer 100D also uses a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery rather than the more common lithium-ion ones, meaning it’s theoretically both safer and longer-lasting, with Jackery claiming it has an up to 8-year lifespan and will retain at least 80% of its capacity across 3,000 charging cycles.
 It has two 140W USB-C ports and an 18W USB-A port, so you can charge, for example, a laptop, phone, and tablet all at once. That said, it tops out at 158W of combined charging power, so you can’t use all of those ports at full power simultaneously.

TechRadar Verdict
 The Anker Solix S2000 made a strong first impression by being useful immediately. Starting at 59%, it covered my intermittent vacuum use throughout a working day and finished with charge remaining.
Its biggest strengths are that useful battery capacity, sensible socket layout and an app that makes the controls understandable. The output ceiling needs consideration, but for compatible equipment, DIY jobs and household backup, there’s plenty to like.

 Portable power stations are useful for everything from keeping your broadband running during a power cut to powering equipment away from a convenient socket. The Anker Solix S2000 fits both roles, combining a substantial battery with a relatively compact upright design.
 What impressed me most, though, was how little fuss it involved. It handled repeated sessions with a 1,200W wet/dry vacuum straight out of the box, while the accompanying app was easy to set up and refreshingly clear about what its settings actually do.

 Design and connections 
 The S2000 has an understated appearance: a dark grey enclosure, rounded edges and a glossy front panel. It looks perfectly at home beside a desk, although mine was soon earning its keep around DIY equipment.
 Its upright shape gives it a reasonably small footprint. At 16.2kg, however, “portable” still involves a deliberate lift. Moving it between rooms or taking it out to the garden is one thing; carrying it a long distance is another.
 The UK version has four proper Type G sockets, split evenly between the front and rear. That arrangement makes sense. You can keep regularly connected equipment plugged in behind the unit, leaving the front sockets available for things you connect occasionally.
 There is a trade-off: you’ll need access to both sides if you want to use every socket. Bear that in mind before squeezing it into a tight space, and leave the ventilation clear.
 Are you a pro? Subscribe to our newsletter
 Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
 The USB connections sit above the display. The 100W USB-C port is the one to choose for a compatible laptop, while the other USB-C connection is limited to 15W. They look similar, so it’s worth checking the labels.
 The screen puts the remaining battery percentage front and centre, alongside input and output wattage and an estimated remaining time. That gives you the information you need without reaching for your phone.
 Performance: a proper day’s work 
 My S2000 arrived with a 59% state of charge. Rather than charging it fully before doing anything useful, I put it straight to work powering a 1,200W wet/dry vacuum.
 Between approximately 10am and 5pm, I used the vacuum repeatedly in sessions lasting around five to ten minutes. The Anker handled those sessions without any problems, and by the time I finished, it still showed 13% remaining.
 To be clear, that was intermittent use across a seven-hour working day, rather than seven hours of continuous vacuuming. Even so, it was a useful practical test: repeated use of a fairly demanding appliance, starting with little more than half a battery.
 The benefit was simple. I could get on with the job without running an extension lead back to a mains socket, and the power station had enough charge to cover the work I needed to do.
 This wasn’t a controlled capacity test. I didn’t record the vacuum’s total running time or measure the energy delivered at the socket, so it wouldn’t be fair to calculate an efficiency figure from the percentage drop.
 What I can say is that it coped comfortably with this particular vacuum and pattern of use.
 The main limitation is the 1,500W continuous output. Battery capacity tells you how much energy is stored; output determines which appliances it can run. A large battery doesn’t automatically mean it can power a typical high-wattage UK kettle or several demanding tools together.
 Check appliance ratings, allow for starting demands, and remember that the output limit is shared across the AC sockets.
 Charging options 
 (Image credit: Future) For everyday charging, the S2000 connects directly to the mains using the supplied AC cable. There’s no separate external power brick to find space for.
 During one charging session, the front display showed approximately 1,068W going in. An app screenshot taken during charging showed around 1,077W, with UltraFast charging switched off. These are snapshots rather than a timed charging test, but they show a substantial charging rate in normal use.
 There’s also an app-controlled UltraFast option when a quicker turnaround matters.
 Away from home, the S2000 supports compatible solar panels and vehicle charging, provided you have the correct cables and accessories. Solar input is capped at 400W, with Anker specifying a maximum open-circuit voltage of 60V. Panel compatibility matters as well as the connector.
 Those alternatives add flexibility, although a normal car accessory socket will be much slower than mains charging. Think of it as a way to replenish charge while travelling, rather than expecting a quick refill of a 2kWh battery.
 The app: easy to set up, easy to understand 
 (Image credit: Future || Anker) The app was one of the nicest surprises.
 Finding it in the Google Play Store was straightforward, as were signing in and getting started. The S2000 was detected straight away, added without difficulty and ready to control. An iPhone version also appears to be available, although my experience here was with Android.
 The main screen presents the battery percentage, temperature, charging estimate and power flow clearly. You can see what’s happening at a glance.
 More useful still is the depth of control. There are multiple UPS and power-management modes, charging timers, adjustable AC charging power and battery charge limits. You also get AC output scheduling, a countdown to switch the sockets off, screen controls and power-usage history.
 Crucially, the explanations are good. Rather than leaving you to decipher a vaguely named mode, the app helps you understand what a setting does and decide whether it suits your needs.
 Some power-station apps make configuration feel like educated guesswork. Here, the guidance makes the extra features more approachable, particularly if this is your first battery system.
 Backup power and everyday use 
 The UPS function adds another potential role: keeping suitable equipment powered when the mains fails. Anker quotes a transfer time of around 10ms, although I haven’t independently measured that or tested compatibility with individual computers.
 For a home office, the combination of rear sockets, battery monitoring and configurable operating modes is appealing. You can leave equipment connected and manage the unit without constantly handling it.

 A couple of decades ago, in a world before pandemics and video calls, the now achingly Gen X phrase ‘road warrior’ was coined to apply to the new breed of perpetually mobile workers. Enabled and emboldened by tech – both in terms of gadgets and the soaring scope of the industry itself – road warriors saw themselves at the vanguard of the new post-office landscape.
 Acer Swift Blade 14 laptop
 (Image credit: Acer)
 The pandemic put paid to any lingering glamour and the vast majority of modern remote workers have swapped the road for the kitchen table, with the occasional coffee shop if funds allow. But the idea of being rootless and restless, whilst remained tethered to co-workers and a career is still an attractive one, even if it often comes out of necessity rather than desire.
 Flowtica Scribe and Folio AI notetaking pen
 (Image credit: Flowtica)
 We’ve scoured the stores to find the best tech accessories for keeping up to date and on the ball when you’re out and about, whether it’s the perennial problem of having enough battery life on hand, or the myriad promises of AI -powered productivity boosts. Here’s our guide to gear for running an office on the move.
 Acer Swift Blade 14 
 Acer
 Swift Blade 14
 £1049.99 
 SHOP NOW 
 One of the thinnest and lightest laptops on the market, the new Acer Swift Blade 14 weighs in at just 799 grams. With a 14” OLED screen, 50Wh battery and Intel Core Series 3 processors (up to the Core 7 processor 350), along with 512GB of storage and 12GB of memory, the Swift Blade 14 is our choice of ultra-lite, providing you’re able to live with one of the two finishes, Marshmallow White and Marshmallow Blue.
 There’s also four-speaker audio, three USB-C connectors and an easily switchable webcam. The 14’s overall thickness of just 12.9 mm makes this an easy addition to the smallest of bags.
 Acer Swift Blade 14, from £1,049.99, Store.Acer.com 
 Krafted Edge 
 Krafted

 £149.99

 Pairing well with the Swift Blade 14 is the Krafted Edge, an ultra-slim laptop powerbank designed to slot beneath the device itself. Just 12mm thick, the Edge has 20,000mAh capability, enough for up to three full laptop charges or four phone charges. Charging the Edge itself should take around two hours and there are two USB-C slots and two USB-A slots for simultaneous device charging.

 Krafted Edge ultra slim power bank

 The battery itself is modular and replaceable, while the casing combines an aluminium alloy base with a top panel made from OBP-certified ocean-plastic (i.e. waste that would otherwise have been ‘Ocean Bound Plastic’). The design cleverly incorporates a braided USB-C cable that slots into one end of the case so you’re never without a means of charging. Perfectly shaped to slot into a laptop sleeve alongside your computer, you won’t even know that it’s there.
 Krafted Edge power bank, £149.99, Kraftedtech.com 
 Lexar Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD 
 Lexar Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD
 (Image credit: Lexar)
 The new Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD from Lexar is designed to bulk up the data capability of your smartphone. Described as the world's thinnest portable SSD, this pocketable storage measures just 8cm by 4.8cm by 3.8mm – it’s only 1 mm thick at some points). Available in 512GB and 1TB sizes, it weighs in at 26.5g and there’s a magnetic sleeve accessory for clipping it to the back of your phone.
 Lexar Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD, available soon, Lexar.com 
 Timekettle LiveTalk 
 Timekettle
 Livetalk Ai Translation Earbuds
 $109 
 SHOP NOW 
 Timekettle have a pair of AI-equipped earbuds out in the wild, the W4 Plus and the LiveTalk. The former more focused on translation, while the LiveTalk is the choice for everyday translation and conversation summaries. Like all products of this ilk – and there are now a lot of them – there’s a certain amount of commitment required to get the best performance. LiveTalk consists of a pair of 6.9g open-ear earbuds that offer real-time AI translation, along with with AI-powered conversation summaries.
 They do work, after a fashion, although the system struggles to keep up with the speed of casual conversation and works best when translating a piece of recorded speech. The sci-fi dreams of genuine real-time, UN-grade machine-driven simultaneous translation are not here yet, but they will be. LiveTalk can be used via your phone’s microphone or by joining in on a phone call.
 Timekettle LiveTalk AI Translation Earbuds
 (Image credit: Timekettle)
 Battery life is an impressive 35 hours (with the relatively hefty case) and as always there’s a subscription service for heavy users who need more than the basic 200 free minutes a month. Occasional travellers will find the LiveTalk’s arsenal of 54 languages (all European languages along with including Chinese, Japanese and Hindi and many more) spans most of the globe.

 Flowtica Folio 
 Flowtica Folio and Scribe AI notetaking pen
 (Image credit: Flowtica)
 Adopting a new workflow doesn’t always feel intuitive, plus there’s the very real danger of switching over to a system or technology that flails, fails or gradually fades into obsolescence.  Watt-Hours (Wh): Why This Number Matters Most

 For reference: a phone charge uses about 15Wh, a MacBook Pro charge uses about 70 to 100Wh, a CPAP night without humidifier uses roughly 300 to 400Wh, and a small fridge uses about 500 to 800Wh over 24 hours. Match the Wh rating to your expected daily load, not your peak load.
 USB-C Power Delivery: 100W, 140W, and What PD 3.1 Means
 USB-C Power Delivery (PD) is the protocol that negotiates fast charging between a charger and a device. The original PD spec topped out at 100W, which is enough for most laptops. USB-C PD 3.1 extends the ceiling to 240W, and 140W ports are now common on premium units like the Anker SOLIX C300.
 For a 13-inch or 14-inch laptop, 100W USB-C is sufficient. For a 16-inch MacBook Pro, 140W charges noticeably faster. Anything below 100W will charge a high-end laptop slowly or not at all, which is why this roundup enforces a 100W minimum.
 LiFePO4 vs Lithium-Ion: Cycle Life and Safety
 LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate) cells deliver 3000 to 6000 charge cycles before significant capacity loss, versus 500 to 800 cycles for standard lithium-ion. LiFePO4 is also more thermally stable and less prone to thermal runaway, which is why every premium unit on this list, Jackery, EcoFlow, Anker, BLUETTI, DARAN, and powkey, uses it.
 Lithium-ion still appears in budget travel banks like the Paopaoyu because it packs slightly more energy per pound. The tradeoff is shorter life and more safety risk. For anything you plan to keep for more than two years, insist on LiFePO4.
 TSA and FAA Airline Compliance: The 100Wh Rule
 The FAA allows lithium battery packs up to 100Wh in carry-on baggage without airline approval, and packs from 100Wh to 160Wh require airline approval at check-in. Packs above 160Wh are prohibited on passenger aircraft. The TSA follows the same thresholds.
 This means the DARAN (89.6Wh), powkey (96Wh), and Paopaoyu (98Wh) are all carry-on legal without approval. The Anker SOLIX C300 (288Wh) requires approval and may be refused on smaller regional carriers. Always check your specific airline, and never pack a power station in checked baggage.
 AC Inverter Wattage and Surge Power
 AC inverter wattage determines what appliances you can run. A 300W inverter (Anker C300) handles laptops, phones, and lights. A 1000W inverter (BLUETTI AC70) adds blenders and coffee makers. A 1500W to 1800W inverter (Jackery, EcoFlow, BLUETTI AC180) covers microwaves, kettles, and most kitchen appliances.
 Surge power, sometimes called peak or Power Lifting, handles the brief startup spike of motors and compressors. A fridge may need 2000W surge even though it draws 150W running. Always check surge rating, not just continuous wattage.
 Safety Features: BMS, Certifications, and Warranty
 A modern Battery Management System (BMS) monitors temperature, voltage, current, and short circuits across every cell. The Jackery ChargeShield 2.0 stacks 62 protection points, the DARAN covers 12, and every unit on this list includes some form of BMS. Avoid any unit that does not advertise a BMS.
 Look for UL, FCC, CE, or UN38.3 certifications as third-party safety validation. Warranty length is a quality signal: Anker and EcoFlow lead with 5-year terms, BLUETTI offers 2 to 5 years depending on model, and budget units typically offer 1 year.
 FAQs
 Is a 100W portable power station good?
 Yes. A 100W USB-C portable power station is enough to fast-charge most laptops, including 13-inch and 14-inch MacBook models, phones, tablets, drones, and cameras at full wall-outlet speed. The 100W threshold matches USB-C PD spec, which is the standard for laptop fast charging. Units with higher AC inverter wattage (1000W and up) can also run small kitchen appliances.
 What is the most reliable portable power station brand?
 Jackery, EcoFlow, Anker, and BLUETTI are the most reliable brands in 2026, based on warranty length, user review volume, and battery chemistry. Jackery and EcoFlow lead for large-capacity units, Anker dominates the compact travel category, and BLUETTI covers the mid-range. All four use LiFePO4 cells rated for 3000-plus cycles and offer 2 to 5 year warranties.
 Which one is better, Jackery or EcoFlow?
 Jackery wins on port selection with two true 100W USB-C ports and lighter weight for its capacity. EcoFlow wins on AC inverter power (1800W with X-Boost to 2600W) and faster UPS transfer times under 10ms. For laptop charging and camping, Jackery is the better pick. For home backup and high-wattage appliances, EcoFlow has the edge.
 What is the best 100W power bank?
 The best 100W power bank depends on use case. For travel under the FAA 100Wh limit, the DARAN 89.6Wh and powkey 96Wh are the top picks. For light camping and daily laptop charging, the Anker SOLIX C300 with 140W USB-C is the value leader. For home backup and off-grid power, the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 and EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic are the best choices.
 Is 100W USB-C good?
 Yes. 100W USB-C is the established standard for laptop fast charging under the USB-C Power Delivery specification. It delivers enough power to charge a 14-inch or 16-inch MacBook Pro at full wall-outlet speed. USB-C PD 3.1 extends the ceiling to 240W, and 140W ports (like the Anker SOLIX C300) charge large laptops even faster, but 100W remains the practical threshold for laptop-class charging.
 Final Verdict: Which 100W USB-C Power Station Should You Buy?
 After testing all eight units, the right pick depends almost entirely on how much energy you need to carry. If you want maximum capacity and dual 100W USB-C ports for serious off-grid or home-backup work, the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is the editor’s choice. If you prioritize AC inverter muscle and UPS functionality, the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic is the better fit.
 If your priority is the best balance of portability, fast USB-C charging, and price, the Anker SOLIX C300 with its 140W USB-C port is the value pick. And if you need a true 100W USB-C portable power station that clears the FAA carry-on limit, the DARAN 89.6Wh and powkey 96Wh are the budget-friendly travel choices that earned their spots on this list.
 The best portable power stations with 100W USB-C in 2026 all share three traits: LiFePO4 chemistry, genuine USB-C PD output that hits the advertised wattage, and a BMS that protects the cells under real-world loads. Pick the capacity tier that matches your daily energy needs, verify the FAA compliance if you fly, and you will end up with a unit that lasts for years.

 The BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 is the best compact portable power station overall because it pairs 288Wh with 600W AC output and 200W solar input at 9.48 pounds.
 The EcoFlow RIVER 3 is the lightest pick at 7.8 pounds, while the Anker SOLIX C300 AC has the strongest USB-C setup for laptops and other travel tech.
 These 245–288Wh stations suit device charging and short light-load jobs, not long refrigerator runs or whole-home backup.

 The BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 is the best compact portable power station for most people . It stores 288Wh, delivers 600W of continuous AC output, accepts up to 200W of solar input, and still weighs only 9.48 pounds. That gives it more useful headroom than the other two without turning it into a heavy camping battery.
 Choose the EcoFlow RIVER 3 when every pound matters. It weighs 7.8 pounds and works well for phones, a laptop, lights, a router, camera gear, or other loads that stay below its 300W rating. The Anker SOLIX C300 AC is the better laptop-charging hub: two of its three USB-C ports can each deliver up to 140W.
 This is a researched, specification-verified guide, not a claim of hands-on testing. We limited the list to current US models with 245–288Wh batteries, AC outlets, LiFePO4 cells, and a listed weight below 10 pounds. That narrow scope keeps the recommendations genuinely portable.

 The tradeoff is that it cannot connect directly to an expansion battery. Its 288Wh capacity is fixed, so buy a larger station if runtime matters more than carry weight. Our BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 vs EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus Wireless comparison covers the closest expandable alternative.
 Best for: Campers and outage kits that need the most AC and solar capability without crossing 10 pounds.
 Best for USB-C: Anker SOLIX C300 AC

 The C300 AC is the best pick when the station will charge laptops, tablets, cameras, and phones more often than AC appliances. Two USB-C ports deliver up to 140W each, while a third provides 15W.  It also has three AC outlets, a built-in light, a car socket, app control, and an under-10ms UPS specification. The tall 6.5-by-6.3-inch footprint takes little floor or desk space, although its 9.5-inch height can be awkward under a shelf.
 Its limitation is output beyond USB-C. The inverter is rated at 300W and solar input tops out at 100W, both well below the BLUETTI. Make sure you are looking at model A1722 , the AC-outlet C300 in this guide. The smaller C300 DC is a different product with no AC outlets. Our Anker SOLIX C300 comparison explains that distinction in more detail.
 Best for: Laptop-heavy travel, mobile work, and charging several USB-C devices efficiently.
 Lightest Pick: EcoFlow RIVER 3

 The RIVER 3 is the easiest model here to carry. At 7.8 pounds, it saves 1.3 pounds over the Anker and 1.68 pounds over the BLUETTI. Its flatter 10-by-8.3-by-4.4-inch shape also slides into a packed vehicle or storage bin more naturally than Anker's tall body.
 EcoFlow gives it a 245Wh battery, 300W rated AC output, one 100W USB-C port, two USB-A ports, two AC outlets, and a car socket. It accepts up to 110W of solar and has a one-hour wall-recharge claim. That is enough for a basic camping electronics kit or short router-and-light backup without carrying extra inverter capacity you will not use.
 The compromises are the smallest battery here, one fast USB-C port, and no expansion connection. The RIVER 3 vs RIVER 3 Plus comparison is worth reading if 600W output, 220W solar input, or extra-battery support matters more than saving 2.6 pounds.
 Best for: Lightweight camping, photography, and predictable small loads below 300W.
 What Can a 245–288Wh Power Station Run?
 These stations are a step above an airline-friendly power bank, not miniature home batteries. They make sense for phones, laptops, cameras, lights, a router, a fan, and short runs of a compact fridge or other modest appliance. The BLUETTI's 600W inverter expands the list of compatible loads, but its 288Wh battery does not make those loads run for long.
 Do not estimate runtime by dividing the label capacity by an appliance's wattage and treating the result as guaranteed. AC conversion, standby draw, temperature, battery protection limits, and appliance cycling all reduce or change real runtime. If a refrigerator, heater, kettle, or medical device is essential, check its running and startup requirements and leave a margin below the station's continuous rating.
 For charging a phone or laptop on a flight, a smaller battery is easier and airline rules matter. Our best power banks for travel guide covers that category. These power stations belong in a car, campsite, or home backup kit; they should not be packed for air travel.
 Which Compact Power Station Should You Buy?
 Buy the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 by default. It delivers the strongest continuous AC output and solar input in this weight class while keeping two useful USB-C ports.
 Choose the Anker SOLIX C300 AC when two 140W USB-C outputs matter more than inverter or solar capacity. Choose the EcoFlow RIVER 3 when minimizing weight is the priority and your loads will stay comfortably below 300W.

 How to Choose a Portable Power Station for Laptop Camping
 Buying a power station for laptop camping requires understanding a few technical concepts that general camping guides often gloss over. The most important factors are capacity in watt-hours, USB-C PD wattage, inverter output, battery chemistry, and recharge speed. Here is how to think through each one for your specific laptop and camping style.
 How Many Watts Your Laptop Actually Draws
 This is the single most important number to know before buying a power station. Different laptop types have vastly different power requirements. An ultrabook like the MacBook Air draws 30W, a standard work laptop like the Dell XPS 13 pulls 45 to 65W, a MacBook Pro 14-inch wants 65W, and a gaming laptop or mobile workstation can demand 180W to 240W from its charger.
 Check your laptop’s power brick for its output wattage. That number tells you the maximum the laptop will draw while charging and under heavy load. Your power station’s AC output or USB-C PD rating needs to meet or exceed that number, or the laptop will charge slowly, intermittently, or not at all. For USB-C charging specifically, the station’s USB-C PD wattage must match or exceed your laptop’s USB-C input requirement.
 Calculating Runtime: Watt-Hours Divided by Laptop Draw
 Runtime is simple math once you know your laptop’s wattage. Divide the station’s watt-hour capacity by your laptop’s power draw, then multiply by 0.85 to account for inverter efficiency losses. For USB-C direct charging, the efficiency is closer to 0.90 since you bypass the AC inverter.
 Here are real examples from our testing. A 65W laptop running off a 1070Wh Jackery 1000 v2 gets roughly 14 hours via the AC outlet (1070 divided by 65, times 0.85). The same laptop on a 292Wh Jackery Explorer 300 gets about 3.8 hours. A 100W laptop on the 999Wh GRECELL gets about 8.5 hours. These are the numbers that should drive your capacity decision, not marketing claims.
 If you work a full 8-hour day, you need a station that delivers at least 610 watt-hours usable (8 hours times 65W, divided by 0.85 efficiency). That points toward the 640Wh LIBRIDS C600 as the minimum for a full ultrabook workday, with the 1000Wh-class stations providing comfortable headroom.
 LiFePO4 Versus Standard Lithium-Ion Battery Chemistry
 Battery chemistry determines how long your power station lasts and how safely it behaves in extreme conditions. LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate) batteries offer 3,000 to 4,000-plus charge cycles before degrading to 70 to 80 percent capacity, which translates to roughly 10 years of typical use. They are also more thermally stable, meaning they handle hot car interiors and cold tent nights better than standard lithium-ion cells.
 Seven of the eight stations in this guide use LiFePO4 chemistry. The GRECELL 1000W uses standard lithium, which is part of how it achieves its lower price. Standard lithium-ion still works fine for laptop charging, but expect a shorter lifespan (typically 500 to 1,000 cycles) and more sensitivity to temperature extremes. If you camp in very hot or cold conditions, LiFePO4 is worth the premium.
 USB-C Power Delivery Wattage Explained
 USB-C Power Delivery has become the primary laptop charging standard, but not all USB-C ports are equal. A port rated at 60W will charge most ultrabooks but struggle with a MacBook Pro 16-inch that wants 100W or more. A 100W port covers nearly all non-gaming laptops. The Anker SOLIX C300’s 140W port is the only option here that matches the fastest USB-C charging available on any device.
 Charging via USB-C is more efficient than using the AC outlet with your laptop’s wall brick, because you skip the inverter conversion step entirely. If your laptop supports USB-C charging and your station has a sufficiently powerful USB-C PD port, use it. You will get 10 to 15 percent more runtime from the same battery capacity.
 Solar Panel Sizing for Laptop Workflows
 Solar charging extends your off-grid laptop runtime indefinitely, but only if the panel is sized correctly. A 100W solar panel in good sun produces about 60 to 70W of actual charging power after conversion losses. To refill a 300Wh station in a day of camping (roughly 5 to 6 peak sun hours), a 100W panel is adequate. To refill a 1000Wh station in a day, you need 200W to 400W of panels.
 Match your solar input to your daily laptop power consumption. If you burn through 300Wh per workday, a single 100W panel can replace that on a sunny day. If you consume 500Wh or more, plan for multiple panels or accept that solar will only partially refill the station between work sessions.
 Weight and Portability Tradeoffs
 Every pound matters when you are carrying gear to a campsite. The lightest station here (VTOMAN at 7 pounds) and the heaviest (Anker C1000 Gen 2 at 24.9 pounds) represent a 3.5x weight difference. The tradeoff is capacity: the VTOMAN holds 230Wh while the Anker holds 1024Wh.
 For car camping where the station stays in or near the vehicle, weight is less critical and capacity should drive your choice. For tent camping, paddle trips, or hike-in sites, prioritize weight and accept shorter runtime. The Jackery Explorer 300 at 7.5 pounds with 292Wh is an excellent compromise for mobile campers who still want 100W USB-C laptop charging.
 FAQs
 What is the best portable power station for camping with laptops?
 The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is our top pick for camping with laptops, offering 1070Wh of capacity, 1500W AC output, and a 100W USB-C PD port. It provides roughly 10 to 14 hours of laptop runtime depending on your machine, recharges in about one hour in emergency mode, and uses long-lasting LiFePO4 battery chemistry. For budget-conscious buyers, the GRECELL 1000W offers nearly identical capacity at a lower price.
 How many watts do I need to run a laptop while camping?
 Most ultrabooks draw 30 to 65 watts, standard work laptops pull 65 to 100 watts, and gaming or workstation laptops demand 180 to 240 watts. Your power station’s AC output or USB-C PD rating must meet or exceed your laptop’s charger wattage. A station with at least 100W USB-C PD output covers nearly all non-gaming laptops for direct USB-C charging.
 Can a portable power station run a laptop?
 Yes, a portable power station can run a laptop as long as it has either an AC outlet (used with your laptop’s wall charger) or a USB-C PD port rated high enough for your laptop. Standard USB power banks cannot run most laptops because they lack AC output and sufficient wattage. Look for a station with at least 300Wh capacity and 100W USB-C PD or 300W AC output for reliable laptop charging.
 How long will a portable power station run a laptop?
 Runtime depends on the station’s watt-hour capacity and your laptop’s power draw. To calculate it, divide watt-hours by laptop wattage and multiply by 0.85 for inverter efficiency. A 1070Wh station runs a 65W laptop for about 14 hours, while a 292Wh station runs the same laptop for about 3.8 hours. USB-C direct charging is roughly 10 to 15 percent more efficient than using the AC outlet.
 What size portable power station do I need for camping with laptops?
 For a full 8-hour workday with a 65W laptop, you need at least 640Wh of capacity (LIBRIDS C600 or larger). For intermittent use or half-day sessions, 300Wh to 500Wh is sufficient. For all-day workstation or gaming laptop use, choose 1000Wh or more (Jackery 1000 v2, Anker C1000 Gen 2, or GRECELL 1000W). Add solar panel capacity if you need multi-day off-grid power.
 Final Verdict: Which Laptop Power Station Is Right for You
 If you need maximum laptop runtime for full workdays off-grid, the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is our Editor’s Choice with the best combination of capacity, fast charging, and proven reliability. Remote workers running 180W-plus workstation laptops should look at the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 for its 2000W AC output and 49-minute recharge.
 If you want near-1000Wh capacity at the best price, the GRECELL 1000W delivers outstanding value. For a balance of mid-range capacity and portability, the LIBRIDS C600 and ALLWEI 500W both offer 100W USB-C charging in lightweight packages. Ultralight campers should choose between the Jackery Explorer 300 and Anker SOLIX C300 depending on whether weight or USB-C wattage matters more.
 For budget buyers who just need a few hours of laptop top-up, the VTOMAN FlashSpeed 300 covers the essentials at the lowest price in this guide. Whatever your laptop and camping style, the best portable power stations for camping with laptops in 2026 are the ones that match your wattage needs, runtime expectations, and weight tolerance. Pick the capacity tier that fits your workday, and let solar panels handle the rest.

 Watt-hours vs watts: how to size a power station
 Every power station has two key numbers. Capacity in watt-hours (Wh) is how much energy the battery stores. Output in watts (W) is how much it can deliver at once. A 1,024Wh unit rated 1,800W can run an 1,800-watt load, but only briefly; it can run a 100-watt load for many hours.
 A labeled rule of thumb for runtime: multiply the watt-hours by about 0.85 to account for inverter losses, then divide by the average watts your devices draw. A 1,024Wh station feeding a 60-watt modem, router and a few LED lights would last roughly 14 hours on that math. Refrigerators cycle on and off, so their average draw is far below their running watts, which is why Anker can claim about 35 hours for a fridge on 2,010Wh.
 Then check surge. Refrigerators, sump pumps and furnace blowers briefly draw several times their running watts when the motor starts. A unit with a low surge rating may trip on startup even if its continuous rating looks adequate. Resistive-load modes like BLUETTI Power Lifting and EcoFlow X-Boost run kettles and heaters at reduced power; they are not true surge capacity.
 Space heaters are the trap. A 1,500-watt heater would drain a 1,024Wh station in well under an hour. If staying warm is the goal, our guide on how to stay warm without power covers better strategies than running resistance heat from a battery.
 Why a power station instead of a generator
 A gas generator stores far more energy in a few gallons of fuel than any battery here, but it has to run outdoors. The CDC says never to use a generator inside a home or garage, even with doors and windows open, and to keep it more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents. The CPSC adds that a porch or carport is too close, and reports nearly 100 consumer deaths a year from portable-generator CO. For apartments, condos, townhomes without a safe 20-foot spot, and anyone who needs power at the bedside, a battery station is the safer tool.
 Many households end up with both. A power station handles the first hours silently and indoors, and a generator outside recharges it or takes over for long outages. The Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus and Anker S2000 listings both describe recharging from a gas generator. If you go that route, the generator rules do not change: outside, 20 feet away, exhaust pointed away from the house, and battery-powered CO alarms inside. See our portable generator roundup for home-backup engines and our inverter generator guide for quieter models that pair well with a battery.
 Battery chemistry, cycles and lithium-ion safety
 Ten of the 13 listings state LiFePO4 (also written LFP) chemistry. LFP is marketed for long cycle life, and several LFP listings here claim around 4,000 cycles before capacity falls to 70 or 80 percent; the ALLWEI claims 3,000. Two listings stand apart: the Anker S2000 at 10,000 cycles and the Jackery 3600 Plus at 6,000. The three listings that do not name LFP (GRECELL, HOWEASY and ZeroKor) all state warranties of two years or less.
 Any lithium battery deserves care. The NFPA advises buying batteries listed by a nationally recognized testing laboratory, using the charging equipment supplied with the device, stopping charging once a battery is full, and taking a device out of service if it shows swelling, unusual heat, odor, popping sounds or color change. Practical points for a power station:
 Charge it where you can see it, on a hard surface, away from beds and curtains.
 Store it partly charged in a cool, dry room; many manufacturers recommend topping it up every few months.
 Do not leave it in a car or an unheated garage through a Colorado winter. Lithium batteries generally should not be charged below freezing unless the manual says otherwise, and capacity drops in cold rooms. The Jackery 3600 Plus listing claims operation down to -4°F; most listings give no low-temperature figure.
 Connecting a power station to house circuits
 Small stations simply power devices plugged into them. Larger stations can back up selected circuits, but only through a proper transfer switch installed by a licensed electrician. Never plug a power station’s AC output into a wall outlet with a male-to-male cord to feed the house. That backfeeds the wiring, and the CDC warns against connecting generators to home circuits without approved devices because a still-connected source can start a fire and endanger utility line workers when power returns. A battery inverter is still a power source on your wiring.
 Jackery describes its MTS manual transfer switch for the HomePower 3600 Plus. Our guide to generator transfer switches explains how the same hardware principles apply. For whole-home, permanently installed batteries tied to solar, compare these units against the systems in our home battery backup roundup .
 Front Range use cases
 Outages along the Front Range tend to follow wind events, heavy wet spring snow and, in some areas, planned utility shutoffs during high fire danger. A few patterns stand out:
 Furnace blower and controls. A gas furnace needs electricity for the blower, inducer and control board. A 1kWh-class station with enough surge may run a furnace blower for a limited time, depending on its draw, but only when connected through a proper transfer switch or furnace-specific setup installed by a licensed technician.
 Sump pumps. Basements in parts of the metro rely on sump pumps during snowmelt and spring storms. A battery station can help, but dedicated systems are often more practical; see our sump pump battery backup guide.
 Medical devices and home offices. A UPS-capable station inline with a CPAP, oxygen concentrator or desktop keeps it running without interruption. Ask your equipment supplier about compatibility.
 Solar recharge. Colorado’s sunny winter days make folding panels practical for topping up between outages.
 If you are buying a home and want an existing transfer switch, battery system or generator inlet checked, get in touch to connect with a vetted local inspector.
 Frequently asked questions
 Can I use a portable power station indoors? Yes. A battery power station has no engine and produces no carbon monoxide, so it can run inside, which is its main advantage over a gas generator. Keep it on a hard surface with clear airflow around the fans, away from beds and curtains, and follow the manufacturer's charging instructions.
 What size power station do I need for a refrigerator? Look for at least 1,000Wh of capacity and continuous output plus surge comfortably above your refrigerator's startup draw. A 1kWh unit may carry a fridge through part of a day; 2kWh units like the Anker S2000 claim around 35 hours. Actual runtime depends on the fridge, door openings and room temperature.
 How long will a power station run a CPAP? Divide the station's watt-hours, times about 0.85 for inverter losses, by the CPAP's average watts. For example, a device averaging 40 watts would get roughly 21 hours from a 1kWh station and about 6 hours from a 300Wh unit. Check the CPAP's rated draw, since heated humidifiers raise it sharply, and ask your supplier about battery use.
 Is a power station better than a gas generator? It is safer and quieter, and it is the only option for indoor use, but it stores much less energy. A generator outdoors can run for days on fuel. Many homes pair the two: the station covers the first hours indoors, and the generator recharges it or carries long outages from at least 20 feet away.
 Can a portable power station back up my whole house? Not on its own in most homes. Even the 3,584Wh Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus is meant for selected circuits through a transfer switch, and only reaches 240V with two units. Whole-home backup usually means a permanently installed battery system or a standby generator.

 How to Choose the Best Portable Power Station for Camping?
 Picking the right portable power station for camping comes down to four key questions: how much capacity you actually need, what battery chemistry you want, how much continuous output your gear requires, and how you plan to recharge. Below is the framework I use when helping friends size their first station.
 Battery Capacity (Wh) and What It Means
 Watt-hours measure how much energy the station can store. A 1,000Wh station can deliver 100W for 10 hours, 200W for 5 hours, or 1,000W for 1 hour. For a typical camp fridge drawing 45W, expect around 18 to 20 hours of runtime from a 1kWh unit, accounting for inverter losses. For phones, lights, and a CPAP, plan on 500Wh to 1,000Wh as a comfortable baseline.
 For backpacking or day trips, 100Wh to 300Wh is usually enough. For family car camping with a fridge, lights, and Starlink, aim for 1,000Wh or more. Real users on camping forums consistently say they wish they had bought more capacity than they originally planned, so when in doubt, size up.
 LiFePO4 vs Lithium-Ion Battery Chemistry
 LiFePO4 batteries last 3,000 to 4,000 cycles before hitting 80 percent capacity, while standard lithium-ion cells typically manage 500 to 1,000 cycles. For a camper who uses a station 30 weekends a year, that difference is the gap between a 3-year and a 13-year service life. LiFePO4 also handles heat and partial state of charge better, which matters when you are leaving the unit in a hot car.
 Every pick in this guide except the GRECELL and ZeroKor uses LiFePO4, and that is intentional. Forum threads are full of stories of lithium-ion power stations swelling or losing capacity by year two, especially in hot climates. If you camp more than a handful of times a year, LiFePO4 pays for itself in longevity.
 Output Power, Ports, and Camping Essentials
 Continuous output matters more than peak surge for most campers. A 1,000W continuous output will run a camp fridge, lights, and a laptop with no problem. A 200W to 300W unit will handle phones, headlamps, and small fans. If you want to run a coffee maker, induction cooktop, or hair dryer, look for 1,500W to 2,200W continuous output with Power Lifting mode.
 Port variety is the other half of the equation. USB-C PD at 100W is now table stakes for laptop charging. A 12V car socket is critical for coolers and tire inflators. Multiple AC outlets let you run a power strip without adapters. The Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 and the BLUETTI AC70 have the best port layouts in this roundup.
 Solar Panel Compatibility and Recharging
 Solar input ratings tell you the maximum watts a station can pull from a panel, but real-world output is usually 70 to 80 percent of the panel’s rated wattage. A 200W panel in good sun will deliver about 140W to 160W. For a 1kWh station, plan on a 200W to 400W panel for a full recharge in a long day.
 Connector type matters. Jackery uses a proprietary 8mm connector, BLUETTI uses XT-60, Anker uses a proprietary Anderson-style connector, and DJI uses a separate MPPT module. If you already own panels, check the connector before buying a new station. The BLUETTI AC70 with its industry standard XT-60 port is the most flexible choice for mixed-brand solar setups.

 What is the best portable power station for camping?

 Is Jackery or Anker better for camping?
 Both are excellent. Jackery has the larger installed base and proven long-term reliability, plus the Explorer 1000 v2 recharges in about 1 hour. Anker’s SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 recharges in 49 minutes, has a 2000W output (versus Jackery’s 1500W), and includes a 5-year warranty. If you need maximum output and fastest charging, go Anker. If you value ecosystem maturity and broad solar support, go Jackery.
 How many watt-hours do I need for a camping power station?
 For solo or duo camping with phones, lights, and a laptop, 300Wh to 500Wh is plenty. For car camping with a fridge, lights, and a CPAP, plan on 1,000Wh. For family trips with a Starlink, induction cooking, or a portable AC, 1,500Wh to 2,000Wh is safer. A 1,000Wh station typically runs a 45W camp fridge for 18-20 hours.
 Can a portable power station run a camp fridge?
 Yes. Most 45W to 60W camp fridges run easily on any 200Wh or larger station. A 1,000Wh LiFePO4 unit will run a typical camp fridge for roughly 18 to 20 hours on a single charge.
